beats.narration_text: The reflex is to hear 'clinical trial protocol skill' and assume Claude is picking the endpoints, sizing the arms, choosing the population. Wrong verb. It drafts the document to a fixed spec — the trial-design calls never leave the human's desk. Here's why that line matters.

beats.narration_text: Take it apart and a skill is just a folder Claude opens before it starts. This one is clinical-trial-protocol-skill. Five files inside: SKILL.md carries the instructions in plain English, a README, and folders for assets, references, and scripts. Claude reads the file, then does what the file says. The file is the program.

Here's what's actually happening. Three steps in a fixed order: read SKILL.md to load the instructions, execute each numbered step from the Steps section, hand back the result. No branching unless a step inside the file explicitly asks for one. They optimized for reproducibility — same input, same run, same shape of output.

The job is narrow on purpose: draft clinical trial protocols for medical devices or drugs when someone asks 'create a clinical trial protocol' or 'help me design a clinical study.' It follows SKILL.md verbatim, so the same request produces the same shape of protocol every run. What's outside the file, it won't touch — the trial-design decisions stay with the person running the trial. That's the trade-off: you lose adaptive judgment, you buy a document you can review the same way twice.

beats.narration_text: Clinical-trial-protocol-skill drafts the protocol to a fixed spec — it doesn't decide how the trial should run; that call still belongs to a person.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to draft a clinical trial protocol for a medical device or drug — the fixed-spec kind that a person still reviews. Read the clinical-trial-protocol-skill, then walk me through the sections it will include and the sections it won't, before you write a single line. Flag any trial-design decisions the skill leaves to me. That way you see the shape of the document — and the shape of the empty space around it — before a single line gets drafted. Go deeper: which parts of a clinical trial protocol — primary endpoint, sample size, inclusion criteria — does the skill compose from my outline, and which parts is it structurally not designed to decide?
